final.title: What subscription sprawl is really hiding
final.body:
Subscription sprawl usually looks like a cost problem, but in a small business it often hides a workflow problem. The real question is not which tool you can cancel. It is which subscription exists because someone is still doing part of the work by hand.

A useful first pass is simple: list every tool, what it is for, how often it is actually used, and which recurring task would stop if it disappeared. That separates active dependencies from legacy extras. The monthly fee matters, but the hidden cost is often owner time wrapped around the tool.

Then pick one repeatable workflow and make the decision concrete. For example, emails arrive, details get copied into a CRM, and another tool is used to chase the next step. If that pattern repeats weekly and the outcome is measurable, it is worth asking whether a bounded automation could handle the routine part. If it is irregular, messy, or tied to medical, legal, high-sensitivity financial, bulk cold-email, scan-heavy OCR-dependent work, or anything that needs unsupported compliance or security guarantees, leave it alone.

Bareni is a one-person consulting practice being built to work inside the customer’s environment. Finished code and customer-named accounts are handed over as policy and no-lock-in positioning, with human approval kept in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

The next step is not to automate everything. It is to write down one recurring workflow and ask whether it is worth diagnosing at all.
